cs.context: Volumetric flow rate. Appears in every calculator. Use the hydraulic/civil engineering term for discharge volume per unit time, not a general word for 'water flowing'.
cs.translation_notes: Spanish has two common terms: 'caudal' (Spain, South America) and 'gasto' (Mexico). Lead with 'caudal'. Portuguese: 'vazão' (Brazil) or 'caudal' (Portugal) — lead with 'vazão'.

cs.context: Ratio of outflow to inflow in a canal reach — measures how much water delivered at the head is received at the tail. Appears in Canal Seepage calculator. E_c = Q_out / Q_in.
cs.translation_notes: This is the most terminology-sensitive term in the suite. 'Conveyance' means transport of water along a canal — do not use a general word for 'efficiency' alone. The term should convey 'how well the canal transports water without loss'.

cs.context: Water lost from a canal through the bed and banks by percolation into the soil. Appears in Canal Seepage calculator.
cs.translation_notes: Use the irrigation/canal engineering term for slow percolation loss, not a word implying leakage through a crack or structural failure.

ds.context: Volumetric flow rate. Appears in every calculator. Use the hydraulic/civil engineering term for discharge volume per unit time, not a general word for 'water flowing'.
ds.translation_notes: Spanish has two common terms: 'caudal' (Spain, South America) and 'gasto' (Mexico). Lead with 'caudal'. Portuguese: 'vazão' (Brazil) or 'caudal' (Portugal) — lead with 'vazão'.

ds.context: Depth of water applied per unit time by a drip or sprinkler system. PR = q / A_e. Appears in Drip/Sprinkler calculator.
ds.translation_notes: In irrigation, 'application rate' or 'precipitation rate' (for sprinklers) or 'irrigation rate'. Use the field irrigation term. Do not use a water-quality or chemical-application connotation.

ds.context: Ratio of minimum to average emitter flow rate in a drip or sprinkler system. DU = q_min / q_avg. Appears in Drip/Sprinkler calculator.
ds.translation_notes: Use the irrigation engineering standard term. 'Uniformity' refers to how evenly water is distributed across the field, not physical evenness of the system.

ds.context: A drip irrigation emitter (dripper/micro-sprinkler) that delivers water at a controlled low flow rate directly to the soil or plant root zone. Appears in Drip/Sprinkler calculator.
ds.translation_notes: May be called 'dripper', 'micro-emitter', or 'emitter' depending on the language and irrigation tradition. Use the field term most familiar to irrigation practitioners in the target language. Where both drip and sprinkler terms exist, prefer the drip term since the calculator covers both.

mi.context: Volumetric flow rate. Appears in every calculator. Use the hydraulic/civil engineering term for discharge volume per unit time, not a general word for 'water flowing'.
mi.translation_notes: Spanish has two common terms: 'caudal' (Spain, South America) and 'gasto' (Mexico). Lead with 'caudal'. Portuguese: 'vazão' (Brazil) or 'caudal' (Portugal) — lead with 'vazão'.

mi.context: Flow velocity (speed of water). Appears in all calculators.
mi.translation_notes: Most languages use a direct cognate of 'velocity'. Do not use a word meaning 'speed' in a general sense if a more precise hydraulic term exists.

mi.context: Cross-sectional flow area divided by wetted perimeter. Appears in Manning calculators.
mi.translation_notes: Standard term in hydraulic engineering — most languages use a direct translation. Do not confuse with 'pipe radius'.

mi.context: Length of the channel or pipe boundary in contact with flowing water. Appears in Manning calculators.
mi.translation_notes: Use the standard hydraulic engineering phrase. 'Wetted' here means 'in contact with water', not 'soaked'.

mi.context: Manning's n — empirical roughness coefficient used in the Manning formula for open-channel and pipe flow.
mi.translation_notes: Always include 'Manning' as a proper noun. The coefficient itself (n) needs no translation — only the label does. Do not translate as generic 'roughness coefficient' without 'Manning'.

mi.context: Dimensionless ratio of vertical drop to horizontal distance (rise/run). Used as channel slope (S_0) and friction slope in Manning and Darcy-Weisbach calculators.
mi.translation_notes: In open-channel hydraulics, 'slope' is the bed gradient — not the angle. Use the civil engineering term for gradient/grade, not a geographic or topographic term.

odt.context: A submerged or free-flowing opening through which water discharges under head. Appears in Orifice Flow and Orifice Drain Time calculators.
odt.translation_notes: In irrigation contexts, often the opening of a headgate or pipe turnout. Use the hydraulic engineering term, not a general word for 'hole' or 'opening'.

odt.context: Coefficient correcting theoretical orifice or weir flow for real-world contraction and friction effects. Appears in Orifice and Weir calculators.
odt.translation_notes: The 'discharge' here refers to flow rate, not the verb. Use the hydraulic engineering compound term.

odt.context: Water surface elevation on the upstream side of a weir or orifice. Appears in Weir Flow and Orifice calculators.
odt.translation_notes: 'Headwater' is an upstream water surface — do not confuse with 'head' (energy) or 'source' (origin of a stream). Use the hydraulic structure term.

odt.context: Water surface elevation on the downstream side of a weir or orifice. Appears in Orifice Flow calculator. When tailwater is above the invert, the orifice is submerged.
odt.translation_notes: Use the hydraulic structure term for downstream water level. Pair consistently with 'headwater elevation'.

keys_to_translate.mphl_note_1:
For an open inlet (culvert) condition, it is necessary to check for inlet control conditions.
1. The upstream HGL cannot be lower than the upstream normal depth flow elevation (or lower than the pipe!).
2. The headwater of a culvert is better represented by the upstream EGL than the upstream HGL.
3. See my 2-minute tutorial for simple standard culvert headwater calculations using HY-8.

HGL a monte in tubazione ' . $ec_lang['mpf_see_notes']; $ec_lang['mphl_note_1']='
Per una condizione di imbocco aperto (tombino), è necessario verificare le condizioni di controllo all'imbocco.
1. L'HGL a monte non può essere inferiore alla quota di deflusso a profondità normale a monte (o inferiore alla tubazione!).
2. Il livello idraulico di un tombino è meglio rappresentato dall'EGL a monte che dall'HGL a monte.
3. Vedere il tutorial di 2 minuti per semplici calcoli standard del livello idraulico nei tombini con HY-8.
